\begin{abstract}

Reserving a local office for women changes who can win it. We compare winners of women-reserved and open seats in rural councils in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Kerala and in the municipal councils of Mumbai and Delhi. Among village heads in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, reserved-seat winners are `r fmt(ss$head_gap[1], 0)` to `r fmt(ss$head_gap[2], 0)` percentage points less likely to hold a university degree. Among Kerala's village council members and in the two cities, graduate shares are about the same. Economic position differs in every village, block and city office with occupation records: reserved-seat winners are `r fmt(es$occupation_gap[1], 0)` to `r fmt(es$occupation_gap[2], 0)` points more likely to report no occupation, and in Rajasthan they declare about `r fmt(-es$rajasthan_assets, 0)`\% fewer assets. In Mumbai and Delhi they are `r fmt(ss$case_gap[1], 0)` to `r fmt(ss$case_gap[2], 0)` points less likely to face a pending criminal case, a record that covers the officeholder but not the male relatives who often act for her. Published comparisons of village heads agree with the rural results: across five independent samples, reserved-seat heads have `r fmt(-lit_meta$d, 2)` standard deviations less schooling.

\end{abstract}

# Introduction

Reserving a seat for women changes who can win it. This paper asks whether the winners of reserved seats are less qualified than the winners of open seats. Open seats can and do elect women, so the comparison is between seat types, not between women and men.

The answer depends on where one looks. Among village heads in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, reserved-seat winners are much less likely to hold a degree. Among Kerala's village council members and the councillors of Mumbai and Delhi, they are not. Setting accounts for most of the variation in the education gap across the six settings we study. Economic position is different: in every village, block and city office with occupation records, including Kerala's and Delhi's, reserved-seat winners far more often report no occupation of their own. In the two cities they are also much less likely to face pending criminal cases.

The rural results match the published evidence. Six studies compare the schooling of village heads in reserved and open seats, and all find less schooling under reservation; pooled, the gap is close to one standard deviation. The pattern in occupation fits a separate body of work showing that male relatives often stand in for women elected under quotas.

# Why these attributes matter

Each attribute candidates declare when they file to run has a claim to shaping how officials govern. Village heads prepare budgets, run public works and allocate benefits, work that requires reading documents, applying rules and dealing with officials [@auerbach, pp. 708–710; @joshi, p. 56]. In South India, more educated council heads target benefits better to landless households and secure fewer for their own [@besleyrewards, Tables 4–5], and graduates who narrowly win Indian state assembly seats raise night-time-light growth in their constituencies [@jaineducation, Table 2], though college-educated leaders do no better across national leaders, US legislators and Brazilian mayors [@carneslupu]. Narrowly electing a state legislator who faces criminal charges lowers growth and road provision [@prakash]. Age shapes incentives: younger Italian mayors facing reelection run larger electoral budget cycles [@alesinaage, Tables 5–7].

Occupation and assets measure economic independence. A winner with no occupation and few assets of her own depends on her household, which is one route by which husbands and fathers-in-law come to exercise the office [@karekurvesood, pp. 1–2; @heinze].

# Existing evidence

Six studies compare the schooling of women-reserved and open-seat village heads (Table \ref{tab:literature}). All find less schooling under reservation: about two to three years where schooling is measured in years [@cd, Table 3; @beaman, Table II; @ban, Table 9], lower completion of secondary school in a national village panel and in Andhra Pradesh [@deininger, Table 3; @afridi, Table 2], and `r fmt(-lit_value("bamezai", "reserved_vs_open"), 2)` standard deviations at Bihar's reservation threshold [@bamezai, Table 7]. On a common scale, the standardized difference in means, and counting the two studies of the same Birbhum councils once, the five samples pool to `r fmt(lit_meta$d, 2)` (95% CI `r fmt(lit_meta$d_low, 2)` to `r fmt(lit_meta$d_high, 2)`). They differ from one another no more than sampling error predicts.

```{r literature-forest, fig.cap="Published comparisons of schooling among elected village heads, women-reserved minus open seats, as standardized differences with 95\\% confidence intervals. Years of schooling are divided by the pooled within-group standard deviation; shares of heads with secondary schooling are converted through the log odds ratio; Bamezai et al. report standard-deviation units. The pooled estimate is a random-effects mean over five independent samples, with the Birbhum councils entered once through Chattopadhyay and Duflo.", out.width="90%"}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("output/meta/forest_literature.png"))
```

Measured against other women in their villages, reserved-seat leaders are positively selected: in Bihar they are more educated than the average woman [@bamezai, Section 7.2.2], in South India they come from wealthier and better-informed households than eligible women [@ban, Table 9], and in Karnataka selection among women is stronger than among men [@moripublished]. In Bihar, the husbands of reserved-seat winners are also less educated than open-seat winners, by `r fmt(-lit_value("bamezai", "husband_vs_open"), 2)` standard deviations [@bamezai, Table 7]. Two further studies compare different groups: reserved women against men in all other seats in Karnataka [@raabe, Table 4], and candidates' standing in their village's education distribution [@mori, Table 3].

# Data and empirical strategy

## Outcomes and samples

The main education outcome is whether the winner holds a university degree; the appendix also reports illiteracy. Unknown qualifications stay missing. Occupation is recorded in Rajasthan, Kerala and Delhi. A winner counts as having no occupation when the entry is nil, unemployed, homemaker or student; pensioners and every named trade or job count as an occupation, and the appendix lists every label with its code. Declared assets come from the nomination affidavits of Rajasthan's 2020 and Uttar Pradesh's 2021 village heads. Pending criminal cases come from MyNeta's affidavit summaries in Mumbai and Delhi and from Uttar Pradesh's 2021 affidavits.

## Specification and inference

For each state, election and office, we estimate

\[
Y_i = \alpha + \beta R_i + \gamma_{g(i)} + \delta_{c(i)} + \epsilon_i,
\]

where $R_i$ indicates a seat reserved for women, $\gamma_{g(i)}$ is a block effect (a district effect where blocks are not recorded throughout) and $\delta_{c(i)}$ is an effect for the seat's caste-reservation class. For binary outcomes, $100\beta$ is the reserved-minus-open difference in percentage points among seats in the same block and caste class. It is the effect of reservation if reservation is as good as randomly assigned within those cells. Standard errors are clustered by block or district, and 95% intervals use a $t$ distribution with one fewer degree of freedom than there are clusters; Kerala's ward and district-member models have only `r num(get_result("Kerala", 2020, "gp_ward")$clusters)` clusters. Mumbai pools its 2012 and 2017 councils with administrative-ward and council effects, clustered by electoral ward, and has no caste-reservation control. Delhi uses assembly-constituency and caste-reservation effects in each election, clustered by assembly constituency.

The administrative records come from state election repositories through [local_elections](https://github.com/in-rolls/local_elections), with input hashes, winner rules, exclusions and coding dictionaries saved in the repository. Bihar's winner is the highest vote-getter, an uncontested candidate, or the winner of a tie drawn by lot; seats whose results form cannot identify a winner are excluded. Kerala's records are of elected ward members, and their reservation refers to the ward even for members who later lead the council.

# Rural panchayats

## Village heads

```{r rural-heads-plot, fig.cap="Graduate-share differences among rural village heads, women-reserved minus open seats, with geography and caste-reservation effects. Bars are 95\\% confidence intervals clustered by geography. UP 2010 uses districts; other rows use blocks. Unclassified education, ambiguous winners and unknown reservation are excluded."}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("output/rural_heads.png"))
```

In Uttar Pradesh, the graduate-share gap is `r contrast(get_result("Uttar Pradesh", 2010, "gp_head"))` in 2010, `r contrast(get_result("Uttar Pradesh", 2015, "gp_head"))` in 2015 and `r contrast(get_result("Uttar Pradesh", 2021, "gp_head"))` in 2021. In Rajasthan it is `r contrast(get_result("Rajasthan", 2020, "gp_head"))` among heads whose qualification can be classified. Many Rajasthan qualifications are recorded only as "Other"; if each could be either a degree or not, the all-winner difference lies anywhere between `r fmt(raj_bounds$all_winners_lower * 100)` and `r fmt(raj_bounds$all_winners_upper * 100)` points.

## Bihar's other offices

Bihar's 2016 records cover `r num(bihar_n$analysis_winners)` elected seats across six village, block and district offices. The graduate-share gap is negative in every office.

```{r bihar-plot, fig.cap="Bihar 2016: graduate-share differences by office, women-reserved minus open seats, with block and caste-reservation effects (district effects for district council members). Bars are 95\\% confidence intervals clustered at that level."}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("output/bihar_2016/education.png"))
```

Bihar's 2021 records add `r num(bihar_2021$analysis_winners)` elected seats with age but not education. Reserved-seat village heads are `r fmt(-head_age(2021)$estimate)` years younger in 2021 (95% CI `r fmt(-head_age(2021)$conf_high)` to `r fmt(-head_age(2021)$conf_low)`), against `r fmt(-head_age(2016)$estimate)` years in 2016. Reservation for 2021 comes from the State Election Commission's feed for the 2021–2026 term, which matches the Commission's count of women-reserved village-head seats.

## Kerala

```{r kerala-plot, fig.cap="Rural Kerala: graduate-share differences by election and office, women-reserved minus open seats, with caste-reservation effects. Block members use block effects and clustering; village and district members use districts. Bars are 95\\% confidence intervals."}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("output/kerala/education.png"))
```

Among Kerala's village ward members, the graduate-share differences are `r contrast(get_result("Kerala", 2010, "gp_ward"))`, `r contrast(get_result("Kerala", 2015, "gp_ward"))` and `r contrast(get_result("Kerala", 2020, "gp_ward"))`. The same office in Bihar shows a gap of `r fmt(-100 * bihar_ward$estimate)` points, so the difference from the northern states is not only a difference between heads and members. Kerala records education as free text; the coding recognizes degrees and school qualifications and leaves incomplete or unrecognized entries missing.

# Urban councils

## Mumbai

Mumbai's councillor records come from the Praja Foundation's report cards and affidavits, as deposited by @mumbaidata. Each councillor enters once per term.

```{r mumbai-plot, fig.cap="Mumbai councillors in the 2012 and 2017 councils: women-reserved minus open seats in graduate share, any pending case and declaring no tax ID (PAN), with administrative-ward and council effects. Bars are 95\\% confidence intervals clustered by electoral ward."}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("output/mumbai/quality.png"))
```

```{r mumbai-values, include=FALSE}
mg <- filter(mumbai, outcome == "educ_grad_plus") %>% rename(estimate = coef_quota)
mc <- filter(mumbai, outcome == "any_criminal") %>% rename(estimate = coef_quota)
mp <- filter(mumbai, outcome == "no_pan") %>% rename(estimate = coef_quota)
```

The graduate-share difference is `r contrast(mg)` and the pending-case difference is `r contrast(mc)`.

## Delhi

Delhi adds the 2012, 2017 and 2022 elections. Winners and assembly mapping for 2012 and 2017 come from Goyal's replication deposit [@delhigoyal]; for 2022, winners come from the OpenCity compilation of Lok Dhaba results and reservation from the State Election Commission's gazette [@delhi2022results; @delhi2022seats, Annexure B]. The 2012 reservation labels match the official schedule [@delhi2012seats, Annexures I–III]. Qualifications and pending cases come from each winner's MyNeta profile [@delhimyneta]; convictions are excluded from pending cases.

```{r delhi-plot, fig.cap="Delhi councillors by election: women-reserved minus open seats in graduate share, reporting no occupation and any pending case, with assembly-constituency and caste-reservation effects. Bars are 95\\% confidence intervals clustered by assembly constituency."}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("output/delhi/quality.png"))
```

The graduate-share differences are `r contrast(get_delhi(2012))`, `r contrast(get_delhi(2017))` and `r contrast(get_delhi(2022))` in 2012, 2017 and 2022. The pending-case differences are `r contrast(get_delhi(2012, "any_criminal"))`, `r contrast(get_delhi(2017, "any_criminal"))` and `r contrast(get_delhi(2022, "any_criminal"))`, and stay negative however the missing case records are filled in.

We do not use the education recorded in the older Delhi files, which is also the coding in Karekurve-Ramachandra and Lee's deposit [@localelections; @delhikarekurve]. For the 2012 winners, its graduate status agrees with the winners' own MyNeta profiles `r fmt(100 * audit$agreement[audit$field == "graduate" & grepl("Delhi", audit$deposit)], 0)`% of the time, about what shuffling the values across winners gives (`r fmt(100 * audit$shuffled[audit$field == "graduate" & grepl("Delhi", audit$deposit)], 0)`%), while the same records' declared assets match `r fmt(100 * audit$agreement[audit$field == "declared assets"], 0)`% of the time. The 2017 education labels agree with the profiles for `r num(delhi_comparison$joint[delhi_comparison$year == 2017] - delhi_comparison$disagreements[delhi_comparison$year == 2017])` of `r num(delhi_comparison$joint[delhi_comparison$year == 2017])` winners. The Mumbai deposit agrees with MyNeta on both education and pending cases.

# Occupation, assets and criminal records

Reserved-seat winners are far more likely to report no occupation of their own, including where their education matches that of open-seat winners. In Rajasthan, `r fmt(100 * es$rajasthan_occupation$estimate, 0)` points more reserved-seat heads report no occupation (95% CI `r fmt(100 * es$rajasthan_occupation$conf_low, 0)` to `r fmt(100 * es$rajasthan_occupation$conf_high, 0)`). Among Kerala's ward members the gap is `r fmt(es$kerala_ward_occupation[1], 0)` to `r fmt(es$kerala_ward_occupation[2], 0)` points across the three elections, and among Delhi's councillors `r fmt(es$delhi_occupation[1], 0)` to `r fmt(es$delhi_occupation[2], 0)` points. Among Kerala's district council members the gap is smaller, `r fmt(es$kerala_district_occupation[1], 0)` to `r fmt(es$kerala_district_occupation[2], 0)` points. Mumbai records no occupation, but reserved-seat councillors there are `r contrast(mp)` more likely to declare no tax ID, all of it in the 2012 council. Counting "social worker" as missing rather than as an occupation moves no estimate by more than `r fmt(ceiling(es$social_shift), 0)` points.

Reserved-seat heads also declare fewer assets: about `r fmt(-es$rajasthan_assets, 0)`% less in Rajasthan and `r fmt(-es$up_assets, 0)`% less in Uttar Pradesh. Criminal records are rare among Uttar Pradesh's 2021 village heads, `r fmt(es$up_crime_rate, 2)`% of those with a known record, and do not differ by seat type (`r fmt(100 * es$up_crime$estimate, 2)` points, 95% CI `r fmt(100 * es$up_crime$conf_low, 2)` to `r fmt(100 * es$up_crime$conf_high, 2)`). The appendix reports every estimate.

# Discussion

The education gap follows the setting. Pooling this paper's estimates with elections nested in settings, reserved-seat village heads in the northern states are `r fmt(-setting_meta$northern[1])` points less likely to hold a degree (95% CI `r fmt(-setting_meta$northern_high[1])` to `r fmt(-setting_meta$northern_low[1])`), against a difference of `r fmt(setting_meta$other_settings[1])` points (`r fmt(setting_meta$other_low[1])` to `r fmt(setting_meta$other_high[1])`) among Kerala's ward members and the two cities' councillors. Distinguishing the two groups cuts the unexplained spread across settings from `r fmt(setting_meta$tau_setting_pooled[1])` to `r fmt(setting_meta$tau_setting_moderated[1])` points. Office, data source and election years vary along with setting, and the second group is one state and two cities. Replacing Bihar's village heads with its ward members, the office we observe in Kerala, still leaves a northern gap of `r fmt(-setting_meta$northern[3])` points.

```{r settings-forest, fig.cap="This paper's graduate-share differences, women-reserved minus open seats, with 95\\% confidence intervals. Pooled estimates come from a random-effects model with elections nested in settings and an indicator for the northern village-head settings.", out.width="85%"}
knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath("output/meta/forest_settings.png"))
```

Where reserved-seat winners match open-seat winners on education, they still differ in economic independence. That is consistent with evidence that male relatives often exercise the office. In a Rajasthan phone audit, 9% of answered calls to reserved-seat village heads reached the elected woman, against 76% in open seats and 31.7% in urban Jaipur [@karekurvesood, pp. 1–2]. Women elected through quotas participate less in council decisions [@heinze], and surveys in two states find male family members prominent in everyday governance [@amar]. For the same reason, the lower rate of pending cases among urban reserved-seat councillors may overstate the change in the office's criminal exposure: affidavits list the officeholder's own cases, not her relatives', and @karekurvelee [p. 11] note that many Mumbai quota women have male relatives who face charges.

Less-qualified winners need not govern worse. In Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, lottery-assigned reservation has no detectable effect on the scale or content of public works [@greensinghsood].

# Measurement and reproducibility

```{r missingness, results='asis'}
coverage <- bind_rows(lapply(c("uttar_pradesh", "rajasthan", "kerala"), function(state) {
  read_csv(file.path("output", state, "descriptive.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(state = state)
})) %>%
  mutate(State = recode(state, uttar_pradesh = "UP", rajasthan = "Rajasthan", kerala = "Kerala"),
         Office = unname(office_labels[tier]), Seat = if_else(quota == 1, "Women", "Open"),
         `Classified (%)` = fmt(100 * education_n / n), N = num(n)) %>%
  select(State, Year = year, Office, Seat, `Classified (%)`, N)
kable(coverage, caption = "Education coverage among eligible winner records. N includes unclassified qualifications.",
      booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE)
```

Education is missing for many winners in Rajasthan, where qualifications are often recorded as "Other", and is classified at different rates across Kerala's seat types. Ages outside 21 to 100 are set to missing. Some Uttar Pradesh inputs come from integration work not yet in a published release of the election data; the repository keeps their byte hashes and the adapter diff.

The missing-education bounds keep the all-winner regression design and let each unclassified winner be either a graduate or not. After reservation is residualized on the controls, the coefficient is a weighted sum of outcomes, so assigning each missing outcome by the sign of its weight gives the exact minimum and maximum. The bounds carry no sampling uncertainty. Uttar Pradesh's bounds are negative in each election; Rajasthan's and Kerala's include both signs.

```{r education-bounds, results='asis'}
bound_table <- bounds %>% mutate(
  State = recode(state, uttar_pradesh = "UP", rajasthan = "Rajasthan", kerala = "Kerala"),
  Office = unname(office_labels[tier]),
  Lower = fmt(all_winners_lower * 100), Upper = fmt(all_winners_upper * 100),
  Missing = num(unclassified), N = num(all_winners_n)
) %>% select(State, Year = year, Office, Lower, Upper, Missing, N)
kable(bound_table, caption = "Missing-education bounds on the adjusted all-winner graduate-share difference (percentage points). These are not confidence intervals.", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE)
```

# Delhi estimates and coverage

```{r delhi-complete, results='asis'}
delhi_table <- delhi %>% mutate(
  Outcome = recode(outcome, graduate_plus = "Graduate or above", illiterate = "Illiterate",
                   age = "Age (years)", any_criminal = "Any pending case"),
  scale = if_else(outcome == "age", 1, 100),
  `Difference [95% CI]` = interval_text(estimate, conf_low, conf_high, scale), N = num(n), G = num(clusters)
) %>% select(Year = year, Outcome, `Difference [95% CI]`, N, G)
kable(delhi_table, caption = "Delhi councillors: adjusted differences in percentage points, except age in years. Assembly-constituency and caste-reservation controls; pointwise intervals clustered by assembly constituency. G denotes clusters.", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE)
delhi_coverage <- read_csv("output/delhi/descriptive.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>% mutate(
  Seat = if_else(quota == 1, "Women", "Open"),
  `Education (%)` = fmt(100 * education_n / n), `Age (%)` = fmt(100 * age_n / n),
  `Cases (%)` = fmt(100 * cases_n / n), N = num(n)
) %>% select(Year = year, Seat, N, `Education (%)`, `Age (%)`, `Cases (%)`)
kable(delhi_coverage, caption = "Delhi outcome coverage among recorded winners. Percentages use all winners of each seat type as the denominator.", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE)
delhi_bound_table <- delhi_missing %>% mutate(
  Outcome = recode(outcome, graduate_plus = "Graduate or above", any_criminal = "Any pending case"),
  Lower = fmt(lower * 100), Upper = fmt(upper * 100), Missing = num(missing), N = num(n)
) %>% select(Year = year, Outcome, Lower, Upper, Missing, N)
kable(delhi_bound_table, caption = "Delhi missing-outcome bounds on the adjusted all-winner coefficient, in percentage points. They carry no sampling uncertainty.", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE)
```
